summary: Jesus opens His great sermon by declaring God’s blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek and the persecuted, and woe to the rich and full.
key_insight: The first and the eighth blessings end with the same promise in the present tense: “theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Everything between sits inside that frame. Jesus describes the people who already belong to the kingdom before He says a word about how they must live.
story: After a night of prayer and the choosing of the Twelve, Jesus came down with them and stood on a level place. A crowd of His disciples was there, and a great multitude from all Judea and Jerusalem and from the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who had come to hear Him and to be healed. Those tormented with unclean spirits were healed as well. The whole multitude sought to touch Him, “for power went out from Him and healed them all.” {Lk}

Matthew says that, seeing the multitudes, Jesus went up on a mountain, and when He was seated His disciples came to Him. Then He opened His mouth and taught them. {Mt} He lifted up His eyes toward His disciples {Lk} and began with blessing.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Then He blessed those who mourn, for they shall be comforted, and the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. He blessed those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. {Mt}

He went on to bless the merciful, who will obtain mercy, the pure in heart, who will see God, and the peacemakers, who will be called “sons of God.” The eighth blessing ended with the same promise as the first: “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” {Mt}

Then He spoke to the disciples directly: “Blessed are you when they revile and persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely for My sake.” They were to rejoice and be exceedingly glad, because their reward in heaven was great, and the prophets before them had been treated the same way. {Mt}

In Luke’s account Jesus speaks to His hearers face to face: “Blessed are you poor, For yours is the kingdom of God.” He blesses those who hunger now and weep now, and those who are hated, excluded and reviled for the Son of Man’s sake. “Rejoice in that day and leap for joy!” {Lk}

Then come four woes, answering the four blessings. “But woe to you who are rich, For you have received your consolation.” Woe to those who are full, for they shall hunger, and to those who laugh now, for they shall mourn and weep. “Woe to you when all men speak well of you, For so did their fathers to the false prophets.” {Lk}
differences: Matthew records eight blessings in the third person (“Blessed are the poor in spirit”) and a ninth spoken to the disciples. Luke records four, all spoken directly (“Blessed are you poor”).
Matthew says “poor in spirit” and “hunger and thirst for righteousness”; Luke says “you poor” and “you who hunger now.” Matthew has “the kingdom of heaven,” Luke “the kingdom of God.”
Luke alone follows the blessings with four woes (Luke 6:24–26).
Matthew sets the teaching on a mountain, with Jesus seated; Luke says He came down with the Twelve and stood on “a level place.”
Only Luke describes the crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon, and the healings before the sermon, when “power went out from Him and healed them all.”

fit.question: Matthew’s sermon is given on a mountain and fills three chapters. Luke’s is given on “a level place,” is about a quarter as long, and includes woes. Are these the same sermon, and if so, why do they differ so much?

points.label: One sermon, two reports
points.text: Most evangelical scholars think so. Both begin with blessings and end with the two builders. The main themes come in the same order. Both are soon followed by Jesus entering Capernaum and healing the centurion’s servant (Matthew 8:5; Luke 7:1). A level place can be a flat stretch on a mountainside, below the summit where Jesus had prayed through the night.

points.label: Each writer selects
points.text: Matthew gathers more of Jesus’ teaching, including much on the Law, the scribes and Jewish practice. Luke, writing for Gentile readers, leaves most of that out and keeps what any reader can take straight into life: blessing, love for enemies, mercy, fruit and obedience.

points.label: A repeated core
points.text: Others, McGarvey among them, think Jesus gave two similar sermons about the same time. A traveling teacher surely repeated His central teaching in many places, and parts of Matthew’s sermon appear elsewhere in Luke in other settings (Luke 11:2–4; 12:22–31).

fit.note: Whether Luke reports the same sermon in shorter form or a second telling of the same core, each writer gives Jesus’ words faithfully and arranges them for his readers.
fit.short: Most likely one sermon: Matthew gives the fuller form, Luke a shorter one for Gentile readers, spoken on a level place on the mountain.

scene.label: The mountain
scene.text: Matthew does not name it. Tradition places it on the hills above the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, where the slopes form natural places for a crowd to sit and listen.

scene.label: Seated to teach
scene.text: Jewish teachers sat to teach, as Jesus did in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:20). The disciples came close, and the crowds listened around them (Matthew 7:28).

scene.label: “Blessed”
scene.text: The word means more than happy. It describes someone God has favored, whatever his circumstances look like. The Psalms open the same way: “Blessed is the man” (Psalm 1:1).

scene.label: Echoes of Isaiah and the Psalms
scene.text: Isaiah 61 promised One anointed to preach good tidings to the poor and to comfort all who mourn, and Psalm 37:11 says, “the meek shall inherit the earth.” At Nazareth Jesus had read Isaiah 61 and said, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).

scene.label: “Woe”
scene.text: The prophets used “woe” as a cry of grief and warning over people headed for judgment: “Woe to those who join house to house” (Isaiah 5:8); “Woe to you who are at ease in Zion” (Amos 6:1). It is a lament and a warning more than a curse.

witnesses.matthew: Sets the King’s first great teaching on a mountain, and many readers hear an echo of Moses receiving the Law at Sinai. Matthew’s “poor in spirit” and “hunger and thirst for righteousness” turn the blessings toward the inner life, and his ninth blessing speaks straight to the disciples.
witnesses.luke: Sets the sermon after a scene of healing, with power going out from Jesus to all who touched Him, as it will again when a woman touches His garment (8:46). Luke gives the blessings as direct address to people who are poor, hungry and weeping “now,” and pairs them with woes on the rich and comfortable. It fits Luke’s concern for the poor, from Mary’s song (“He has filled the hungry with good things,” Luke 1:53) onward.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks blessing with an authority no prophet claimed. He declares whom God favors, gives away the kingdom, and calls suffering “for My sake” a reason for joy.
seeing.living: The kingdom is given to the poor in spirit, not earned by the strong. Come to Jesus with empty hands rather than an impressive record, and when following Him costs you, remember that He called that very thing blessed. Luke’s woes warn the other way: wealth, a full table and everyone’s praise can be all the consolation a person ever receives.
seeing.ponder: Which of these blessings describes you least, and what would it take for Jesus to make it true of you?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus calls blessed the people the world overlooks, and gives them the kingdom.
outline: The King sits down to teach (1–2)
Blessed in their likeness to God (7–9)
preaching.watch_for: The blessings move from the disciple’s need before God (vv. 3–6), to how he treats others (vv. 7–9), to how others treat him (vv. 10–12). At verse 11 Jesus shifts from “those” to “you,” speaking straight to His disciples.
